title: Most animals make their own vitamin C, but a broken gene stops you
body: [Most animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_C) build vitamin C themselves, and the final step needs an enzyme called **L-gulonolactone oxidase**, or GULO. In our primate ancestors the gene for GULO stopped working about 63 million years ago, around the time primates split into two groups. Its battered remains still sit on human chromosome 8 as a pseudogene, a copy riddled with mutations that no longer makes the enzyme. That is why people, like monkeys and apes, have to get vitamin C from food.

slides.heading: Makes its own vitamin C, or needs it in food?
slides.explanation: Lemurs belong to the primate branch that kept a working GULO gene. Guinea pigs lost theirs on a separate branch of the family tree.

left.label: Strepsirrhines
left.text: Lemurs and lorises, the 'wet-nosed' primates. They can still make vitamin C.

right.label: Haplorhines
right.text: Tarsiers, monkeys, apes and humans. GULO is not produced, so vitamin C must come from food.

slides.clue: A broken copy of a gene that still sits in the genome but no longer works
slides.detail: Your vitamin C pseudogene is called GULOP. Guinea pigs carry a similar mutated remnant of the same gene.
